title: The Hallmarks of Cancer
description: Hanahan and Weinberg's organizing framework for malignancy

concepts.title: Six Original Hallmarks (2000)
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2000, Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg published The Hallmarks of Cancer in Cell, arguing that the bewildering diversity of human tumors masks a small set of shared functional capabilities. Their original six: self-sufficiency in growth signals, insensitivity to anti-growth signals, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replicative potential, sustained angiogenesis, and tissue invasion and metastasis.

Each hallmark corresponds to a specific normal regulatory circuit that the cancer cell has subverted. Growth signal autonomy comes from oncogenic activation of receptor tyrosine kinases or RAS. Anti-growth insensitivity comes from RB or p53 loss. Limitless replication is achieved by reactivating telomerase (TERT), normally silenced in somatic cells after embryogenesis.

The framework's power is that it lets clinicians and researchers organize seemingly unrelated mutations under a common functional schema. A KRAS G12D pancreatic tumor and an EGFR L858R lung adenocarcinoma both achieve growth-signal autonomy — different molecules, same hallmark. Drug development now routinely targets specific hallmarks rather than specific tissues.

concepts.title: The Enabling Characteristics and Emerging Hallmarks (2011)
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2011 update added two enabling characteristics that make hallmark acquisition possible: genome instability and mutation, and tumor-promoting inflammation. Without elevated mutation rates, a cell rarely accumulates the half-dozen driver mutations needed for full malignancy in a human lifetime. Inflammation supplies growth factors, survival signals, and reactive oxygen species that themselves accelerate mutation.

Two emerging hallmarks were also added: deregulated cellular energetics (the Warburg effect — aerobic glycolysis even in oxygen-rich conditions, glucose flux 10-100× normal) and avoiding immune destruction. The Warburg shift was first observed by Otto Warburg in the 1920s; we now understand it as supporting biosynthesis, not just ATP production. Immune evasion became the foundation for the checkpoint inhibitor revolution.

This expansion mattered clinically: PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab approved 2014) targeted the immune-evasion hallmark and produced durable remissions in melanoma, lung, and renal cancers that had been essentially untreatable.

concepts.title: The 2022 Revision: Fourteen Hallmarks
concepts.contentHtml:
Hanahan's 2022 update in Cancer Discovery added four more capabilities, bringing the total to 14. The new entries: unlocking phenotypic plasticity (cells revert toward stem-like states or switch lineage, e.g., adenocarcinoma to neuroendocrine after androgen blockade in prostate cancer), nonmutational epigenetic reprogramming (heritable expression changes without DNA sequence changes — DNA methylation, histone modifications), polymorphic microbiomes (gut and tumor-resident bacteria modulating both tumor biology and therapy response), and senescent cells (formerly seen only as tumor-suppressive, now recognized as actively pro-tumorigenic via the SASP — senescence-associated secretory phenotype).

The expanded framework reflects a decade of single-cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and microbiome research. It also reflects therapeutic blind spots — many resistant tumors evade therapy through plasticity rather than new mutations, which is why mutation-targeted drugs eventually fail.

Memorize the framework. It will reappear in every subsequent lesson.

title: Oncogenes and Tumor Suppressors
description: Gain-of-function vs loss-of-function, and the two-hit hypothesis

concepts.title: Oncogenes: Dominant Gain of Function
concepts.contentHtml:
An oncogene is the activated form of a normal cellular gene (a proto-oncogene) that gained function through mutation, amplification, or chromosomal translocation. A single mutated allele suffices — oncogenic activation is genetically dominant.

Three textbook examples. RAS (HRAS, KRAS, NRAS) — a small GTPase that toggles between GDP-bound (off) and GTP-bound (on). Hotspot mutations at codons 12, 13, and 61 (e.g., KRAS G12D, G12C, G12V) lock RAS in the active state, driving constitutive MAPK signaling. KRAS is mutated in ~90% of pancreatic, ~40% of colorectal, and ~30% of lung adenocarcinomas. MYC — a transcription factor amplified or translocated in Burkitt lymphoma (t(8;14) places MYC under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer). EGFR — overexpressed in glioblastoma; activating mutations (L858R, exon 19 deletions) define a major subset of non-small-cell lung cancer.

The mutation pattern is highly stereotyped — the same hotspots appear repeatedly because the protein has very specific residues whose alteration constitutively activates downstream signaling.

concepts.title: Tumor Suppressors: Recessive Loss of Function
concepts.contentHtml:
Tumor suppressor genes normally restrain proliferation, repair DNA, or trigger apoptosis. Their inactivation is typically recessive — both alleles must be lost or silenced. TP53 ("the guardian of the genome") is mutated in ~50% of all human cancers. RB1, the original tumor suppressor identified, gates the G1/S transition. PTEN, a lipid phosphatase, antagonizes the PI3K/AKT survival pathway.

TP53 mutations cluster in the DNA-binding domain — codons 175, 245, 248, 249, 273, 282 are recurrent hotspots. Many mutations are missense, producing a stable but non-functional protein that may even act as a dominant-negative or gain-of-function mutant. This is why TP53 mutations sometimes behave half-oncogene, half-tumor-suppressor — the mutant protein interferes with wild-type p53 from the other allele.

Loss of heterozygosity (LOH) is a key mechanism: a cell with one inherited or somatically acquired mutation loses the wild-type allele through deletion, mitotic recombination, or chromosome non-disjunction. LOH at 17p (TP53), 13q (RB1), and 10q (PTEN) is detectable by sequencing or SNP arrays.

concepts.title: Knudson's Two-Hit Hypothesis
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1971, Alfred Knudson studied retinoblastoma — a rare childhood eye tumor that runs in families. Hereditary cases tended to be bilateral and presented in infancy; sporadic cases were unilateral and presented later. Knudson's two-hit hypothesis: tumorigenesis requires two independent inactivating events at the RB1 locus. Hereditary cases inherit one defective allele in every cell; only one further somatic hit anywhere in the retina produces a tumor. Sporadic cases need both hits in the same cell, an exponentially rarer event.

The math fits the data. If the per-cell-per-year probability of a hit is p ≈ 10⁻⁶, then in a hereditary patient the expected number of tumor-initiated cells in the retina (~10⁷ retinoblasts) over the first few years of life is roughly 10⁷ × p × t — guaranteeing several tumors per eye. In sporadic cases, both hits are needed: ~10⁷ × p² × t, predicting unilateral tumors at low frequency.

The hypothesis generalizes beyond RB1. Hereditary cancer syndromes — Li-Fraumeni (TP53), Lynch (MLH1/MSH2), familial adenomatous polyposis (APC), BRCA1/2 — all follow the same logic. One inherited hit, one somatic hit, then full inactivation.

title: Genomic Instability and Mutational Signatures
description: Mutator phenotypes, BRCA, MSI, and the Alexandrov signatures

concepts.title: The Mutator Phenotype
concepts.contentHtml:
The somatic mutation rate of a normal human cell is roughly 10⁻⁹ per base per division — extraordinarily low, the product of high-fidelity polymerases, proofreading, and post-replicative mismatch repair. At this baseline, accumulating ~5-7 driver mutations in one cell during a lifetime is statistically marginal for an organism with ~10¹⁴ cells.

Lawrence Loeb proposed in 1991 that cancers operate under a mutator phenotype: an early hit disables a DNA repair pathway, dramatically elevating the per-division mutation rate, and the resulting genetic chaos accelerates acquisition of further drivers. The mutator phenotype isn't a hallmark per se — it's the engine that enables hallmark acquisition.

Concrete instances: deficient mismatch repair (Lynch syndrome, MLH1 silencing) raises point mutation rates 100-1000×. BRCA1/2 loss cripples homologous recombination, producing characteristic deletion patterns. APOBEC cytidine deaminase activity, normally an antiviral defense, can run amok and seed thousands of C→T or C→G mutations across the genome. Polymerase epsilon (POLE) proofreading-domain mutations produce ultramutated tumors with >100 mutations per megabase.

concepts.title: BRCA, Microsatellite Instability, and Synthetic Lethality
concepts.contentHtml:
BRCA1 and BRCA2 encode proteins essential for double-strand break repair via homologous recombination. Germline mutations carry a 50-80% lifetime risk of breast cancer and 15-40% risk of ovarian cancer. BRCA-deficient tumors rely heavily on the alternative single-strand-break repair pathway mediated by PARP1.

This dependency creates a synthetic lethality: inhibiting PARP in a normal cell is tolerable (HR backs it up), but inhibiting PARP in a BRCA-mutant cell collapses both repair pathways simultaneously and the cell dies. Olaparib (Lynparza) was the first PARP inhibitor approved (2014) — it transformed treatment for BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer and is now used for breast and prostate cancer with HR-deficiency signatures.

Microsatellite instability (MSI) reflects mismatch-repair deficiency. Microsatellites — short tandem repeats like (CA)ₙ — are particularly hard to replicate accurately; without MMR, their lengths fluctuate. MSI-high tumors carry hundreds of indels, generate many neoantigens, and respond exceptionally well to checkpoint inhibitors. The FDA's first tissue-agnostic approval (pembrolizumab, 2017) was for any MSI-high solid tumor regardless of origin.

concepts.title: Alexandrov Mutational Signatures
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2013, Ludmil Alexandrov and colleagues showed that you can read a tumor's history from the pattern of its point mutations. Each mutagenic process — UV light, tobacco smoke, APOBEC, defective MMR, HR deficiency — leaves a characteristic spectrum of base substitutions in specific trinucleotide contexts. By non-negative matrix factorization on thousands of tumor genomes, they extracted a catalog of mutational signatures (now SBS1 through SBS90+).

Examples. SBS4 — predominantly C→A transversions, the fingerprint of tobacco smoke; ubiquitous in lung cancers from smokers. SBS7a/b — C→T at dipyrimidines, the UV signature, dominant in melanoma. SBS6 — C→T at NpCpG sites, characteristic of MMR deficiency. SBS3 — broad signature with small indels, the BRCA/HR-deficiency signature.

The clinical use case: a tumor with an SBS3 signature but no detected BRCA mutation is still HR-deficient and likely PARP-inhibitor-responsive. The signatures give a functional readout that survives the heterogeneity of which specific gene was hit. The Catalog of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC) hosts the reference signatures and tools to decompose new tumors.

title: Clonal Evolution and Tumor Heterogeneity
description: Linear, branched, and convergent evolution within a single tumor

concepts.title: Nowell's Clonal Evolution Model
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1976, Peter Nowell published a one-page paper in Science proposing that tumor progression is Darwinian: a tumor is a population of genetically variant cells, and selection acts on the variation, favoring the fittest clones. Each new driver mutation produces a subclone that may sweep through the tumor (selective sweep) or coexist with parental clones.

Modern multi-region sequencing has confirmed and refined the model. Tumors are not genetically uniform. A single ~1 cm tumor of ~10⁹ cells contains thousands of distinct subclones differing by hundreds to thousands of mutations. Some mutations are truncal (present in every cell — early events from the most recent common ancestor) while others are branch mutations (present in only some regions).

The TRACERx lung cancer study (Swanton et al., 2017+) sampled multiple regions per tumor at surgery and at recurrence. In lung adenocarcinoma, EGFR and TP53 mutations were typically truncal — early necessary events. Drug-resistance mutations like EGFR T790M were often branch mutations, present at low frequency before therapy and selected for during treatment.

concepts.title: Linear vs Branched vs Convergent Evolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Phylogenetic reconstruction from multi-region sequencing reveals three patterns. Linear evolution: a sequence of selective sweeps, each clone replacing the last. Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia often looks linear. Branched evolution: multiple subclones diverge from a common ancestor and coexist in the tumor at sampling time. Renal cell carcinoma is the canonical example — Marco Gerlinger and Charles Swanton's 2012 paper sampled four regions of a single ccRCC and found that some driver mutations (VHL loss) were truncal but most others varied region-to-region.

Convergent evolution: independent subclones acquire different mutations that hit the same pathway. In one ccRCC tumor, three different SETD2 mutations and two different KDM5C mutations arose in separate branches, all converging on chromatin-regulatory disruption. Convergence is strong evidence that the affected pathway is under positive selection.

This heterogeneity has clinical consequences. A single biopsy may misrepresent the tumor. Targeted therapies select for pre-existing minor clones harboring resistance — and because the tumor was already polyclonal, resistance is essentially inevitable for any monotherapy.

concepts.title: Liquid Biopsy and ctDNA
concepts.contentHtml:
Tumors continuously shed DNA fragments (~167 bp, the nucleosome footprint) into the blood as cells die. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is detectable from a routine blood draw, typically constituting 0.01% to 10% of total cell-free DNA depending on tumor burden. Sequencing ctDNA gives a real-time, less-invasive snapshot of the tumor's mutational landscape — and crucially, an aggregate view that captures multiple subclones simultaneously.

Clinical applications. Minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring: after curative-intent surgery, persistent ctDNA predicts recurrence months before imaging shows it (e.g., the DYNAMIC trial in colorectal cancer). Resistance tracking: in EGFR-mutant lung cancer, ctDNA can detect emergence of T790M (resistance to first-generation TKIs) and trigger switching to osimertinib. Treatment-response monitoring: ctDNA falls within days of effective therapy, faster than RECIST imaging response.

Limitations: ctDNA shedding varies hugely by tumor type. Glioblastoma rarely sheds (blood-brain barrier); lung and colorectal shed reliably. Low-frequency variants need ultra-deep sequencing or molecular barcoding to distinguish true mutations from sequencing errors.

title: The Tumor Microenvironment
description: Stroma, CAFs, ECM, hypoxia, and the tumor as an ecosystem

concepts.title: Cancer-Associated Fibroblasts and Stromal Reprogramming
concepts.contentHtml:
A tumor is not just transformed epithelium — it's an organ-like ecosystem. Up to 90% of cells in a pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma can be non-malignant stromal cells: fibroblasts, immune cells, endothelial cells, pericytes, and adipocytes, all reprogrammed by tumor-derived signals.

Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) arise from resident tissue fibroblasts, mesenchymal stem cells, or epithelial-mesenchymal transition. They secrete TGF-β, FGF, IL-6, and the chemokine CXCL12, which protects tumor cells from cytotoxic T cells. CAFs lay down a dense, cross-linked extracellular matrix — collagen, fibronectin, hyaluronan — that physically excludes immune cells and impedes drug penetration. The desmoplastic stroma of pancreatic cancer is so rigid it generates intratumoral pressures that collapse blood vessels.

Single-cell analyses now distinguish CAF subtypes. myCAFs are myofibroblast-like, ECM-producing. iCAFs are inflammatory, secreting IL-6 and pro-tumorigenic cytokines. apCAFs are antigen-presenting and may modulate T cell responses. Targeting CAFs has been clinically frustrating — broad fibroblast depletion accelerated pancreatic cancer in mouse models, suggesting a tumor-restraining role for some subsets.

concepts.title: Angiogenesis, Hypoxia, and HIF
concepts.contentHtml:
A tumor cannot grow beyond ~1-2 mm without acquiring its own blood supply — diffusion alone won't deliver oxygen and glucose past that distance. Judah Folkman proposed in 1971 that blocking the angiogenic switch — the moment a tumor begins recruiting vessels — would starve tumors. The angiogenic switch is largely driven by VEGF-A, secreted in response to hypoxia.

The hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) pathway is the central oxygen sensor. In normoxia, HIF-1α and HIF-2α are hydroxylated by PHD enzymes (which require O₂), recognized by the VHL ubiquitin ligase, and degraded. In hypoxia, hydroxylation stalls, HIF accumulates, and it transactivates ~100 genes including VEGF, GLUT1, and glycolytic enzymes. The 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology went to Kaelin, Ratcliffe, and Semenza for working this out.

Tumor vasculature, induced rapidly by VEGF, is structurally abnormal — leaky, tortuous, with pericyte coverage gaps. Anti-VEGF therapy (bevacizumab/Avastin, approved 2004) was hyped to revolutionize oncology. Outcomes were modest: it adds months in colorectal and lung cancer combinations but resistance develops via alternative angiogenic factors (PlGF, FGF2). Rakesh Jain's vascular normalization hypothesis explains why low-dose anti-VEGF actually improves drug delivery — pruning excess vessels reduces interstitial pressure and improves perfusion.

concepts.title: Hypoxia, the Warburg Effect, and Metabolism
concepts.contentHtml:
Tumor regions further than ~100 μm from a vessel are hypoxic. Hypoxic cells are radioresistant (radiation kills via ROS, which need O₂), chemoresistant (low blood flow = low drug delivery), and selected for HIF-driven survival programs. They also drive metabolic adaptation: the famous Warburg effect, where tumors preferentially metabolize glucose to lactate even with abundant oxygen.

Why ferment when oxidative phosphorylation yields 16× more ATP? The answer isn't ATP at all — it's biosynthesis. A rapidly dividing cell needs nucleotides, amino acids, and lipids. Glycolytic intermediates feed the pentose phosphate pathway (ribose for nucleotides, NADPH for reductive biosynthesis), serine biosynthesis, and lipid building blocks. Otto Warburg saw the lactate; Lewis Cantley and others reframed it as the cell prioritizing carbon for growth.

The Warburg effect is exploited diagnostically. FDG-PET (¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography) lights up tumors because they import glucose voraciously through GLUT1 and trap FDG-6-phosphate that can't proceed through glycolysis. PET signal intensity (SUV — standardized uptake value) tracks tumor metabolic activity and treatment response.

title: Metastasis and the Seed-and-Soil Hypothesis
description: EMT, circulating tumor cells, dormancy, and organotropism

concepts.title: The Metastatic Cascade
concepts.contentHtml:
Metastasis kills 90% of cancer patients, yet the process is staggeringly inefficient. A 1-cm tumor sheds millions of cells into circulation per day; almost none establish viable metastases. Each step is a filter. Local invasion: cells breach the basement membrane via matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2, MMP-9). Intravasation: cells enter blood or lymphatic vessels, often at leaky tumor capillaries. Circulation: most circulating tumor cells (CTCs) die from shear stress or anoikis — apoptosis triggered by detachment from substrate. Survivors that travel as clusters with platelets or neutrophils have ~50× higher metastatic potential than singletons.

Extravasation: the cell adheres to a distant vascular endothelium and crosses it. Colonization: the rate-limiting step. The cell must survive in foreign tissue, evade immune surveillance, and reinitiate proliferation. Most extravasated cells either die or enter long-term dormancy.

Estimates suggest ~1 in 10⁴ CTCs survives to seed a clinically detectable metastasis. The bottleneck explains why metastasis often takes years and why early-stage tumors are curable by surgery alone in many cases.

concepts.title: EMT, MET, and Phenotypic Plasticity
concepts.contentHtml:
To intravasate, an epithelial cell must lose adhesion, polarity, and apicobasal organization, and gain motility and matrix-degrading capacity. This is the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) — a developmental program (used during gastrulation and neural crest formation) that adult cancers reactivate.

Key transcription factors: SNAIL, SLUG, TWIST, ZEB1, ZEB2. They repress E-cadherin (the principal epithelial adhesion molecule) and upregulate N-cadherin, vimentin, and fibronectin. The trigger is often TGF-β from CAFs or hypoxia-induced HIF activity.

EMT is a spectrum, not a switch. Cells in partial EMT states — coexpressing epithelial and mesenchymal markers — appear most metastatic. Crucially, the reverse process, MET (mesenchymal-epithelial transition), is required for colonization at distant sites. The metastatic cell needs the mesenchymal program to escape and the epithelial program to grow at the new site. Plasticity, not a fixed mesenchymal state, is what's selected for. This is why mesenchymal markers in primary tumors don't always predict metastasis well.

concepts.title: Organotropism and Paget's Seed and Soil
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1889, Stephen Paget noticed something odd: in autopsies of breast cancer patients, metastases didn't distribute proportionally to blood flow. The liver and bones got far more than chance predicted; the spleen, despite high perfusion, got essentially none. He proposed the seed and soil hypothesis: tumor cells (seeds) only grow where the microenvironment (soil) supports them.

Different cancers metastasize to characteristic sites — organotropism. Breast cancer favors bone, liver, lung, brain. Prostate cancer favors bone (lytic + osteoblastic mix). Colorectal cancer favors liver (portal venous drainage delivers it directly). Uveal melanoma overwhelmingly metastasizes to liver. Pancreatic cancer favors liver and lung.

Modern mechanisms: tumor-derived exosomes deliver integrin-laden vesicles that prime the pre-metastatic niche (David Lyden, Joan Massagué labs). Exosomal integrin α6β4 directs lung tropism; integrin αvβ5 directs liver tropism. The soil is also influenced by chemokine gradients — bone marrow CXCL12 attracts CXCR4-expressing cancer cells, explaining bone tropism in breast and prostate cancer. Some metastases enter dormancy for years, single cells or micrometastases that resume growth only when local signals shift (often after surgery or stress).

title: Immune Evasion and Cancer Immunoediting
description: How tumors hide from T cells: MHC loss, Tregs, exhaustion, PD-L1

concepts.title: Immunoediting: Elimination, Equilibrium, Escape
concepts.contentHtml:
The immune system both restrains cancer and shapes it. Robert Schreiber's cancer immunoediting framework (2002) identifies three phases. Elimination: nascent tumors are recognized and destroyed by CD8 T cells, NK cells, and IFN-γ. Most never become clinically detectable — immunocompetent mice develop fewer carcinogen-induced tumors than immunodeficient mice.

Equilibrium: the immune system controls but doesn't eliminate the tumor. The two populations exist in dynamic balance for years, during which selective pressure favors tumor variants that evade detection. This explains anecdotal cases of "transmitted" cancer in transplant recipients — the donor harbored an equilibrium-phase tumor, and immunosuppression let it escape.

Escape: the edited tumor — now selected for poor immunogenicity — outgrows immune control and becomes clinically apparent. By the time a tumor is biopsied, immunoediting has already shaped it. The mutational burden retained in escaped tumors is biased away from neoantigens that elicit strong T cell responses, the genomic fingerprint of past T cell selection.

concepts.title: Mechanisms of Evasion
concepts.contentHtml:
Tumors employ a suite of evasion strategies. MHC class I loss — downregulation or mutation of HLA, β2-microglobulin, or antigen-processing machinery (TAP1, TAP2). MHC-low tumors hide from CD8 T cells but should be vulnerable to NK cells, which recognize "missing self" — except tumors often coopt that too via HLA-E expression engaging the inhibitory NKG2A receptor.

T cell exhaustion: chronic antigen exposure drives CD8 T cells into a hyporesponsive state characterized by sustained expression of inhibitory checkpoints PD-1, CTLA-4, TIM-3, LAG-3, TIGIT. Exhausted cells lose effector function (IFN-γ, granzyme, perforin) and proliferative capacity. Tumors actively reinforce exhaustion by expressing the corresponding ligands, especially PD-L1.

Suppressive cell recruitment: regulatory T cells (Tregs, FOXP3+) infiltrate and suppress effector responses. Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs, often M2-polarized) secrete IL-10, TGF-β, and arginase-1, depleting arginine and crippling T cells. IDO (indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase) catabolizes tryptophan, starving T cells of an essential amino acid and producing immunosuppressive kynurenine.

concepts.title: Neoantigens and Tumor Mutational Burden
concepts.contentHtml:
The reason any tumor can be recognized by T cells in the first place is that mutations create neoantigens — peptides not found in the normal proteome. A nonsynonymous mutation may generate a 9-mer peptide that, if it binds the patient's HLA, can be presented on the tumor cell surface and recognized as foreign by a TCR.

Most mutations don't yield strong neoantigens. Of ~100 nonsynonymous mutations in a typical lung adenocarcinoma, perhaps 5-10 produce HLA-binding peptides, and only a fraction elicit clonally expanded T cell responses. The probability scales with both mutational burden and HLA diversity.

Tumor mutational burden (TMB) — mutations per megabase — predicts checkpoint inhibitor response. Melanoma (UV-driven) and smoking-related lung cancers have TMB of 10-100/Mb and respond well. Microsatellite-unstable colorectal cancers (TMB > 20/Mb) respond well. Pediatric tumors and most prostate cancers have TMB < 1/Mb and respond poorly. The FDA approved pembrolizumab (2020) for any solid tumor with TMB ≥ 10/Mb — another tissue-agnostic approval rooted in mechanism, not anatomy.

title: Cancer Therapeutics: From Cytotoxics to Targeted Agents
description: Chemo, targeted therapy, endocrine, radiation, antibody-drug conjugates

concepts.title: Cytotoxic Chemotherapy and Radiation
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells by interfering with DNA replication or mitosis. Major classes:

Antimetabolites mimic nucleotides. 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) is incorporated as a fluorinated uracil; methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking thymidylate synthesis; gemcitabine terminates DNA strands. Alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide, temozolomide) covalently crosslink DNA. Platinum agents (cisplatin, carboplatin, oxaliplatin) form intrastrand and interstrand DNA crosslinks. Topoisomerase inhibitors (etoposide, irinotecan, doxorubicin) trap topoisomerase-DNA complexes, generating double-strand breaks. Microtubule agents — taxanes (paclitaxel, docetaxel) stabilize microtubules; vinca alkaloids (vincristine) destabilize them; both halt mitosis.

Radiation therapy deposits energy that ionizes water to OH• radicals, breaking DNA. Tumor cells are more vulnerable than normal tissue because they cycle faster and often have impaired DNA repair. Fractionation (small daily doses) exploits the differential repair capacity. Modern techniques — IMRT, proton therapy, stereotactic body radiotherapy — sculpt dose to the tumor while sparing organs at risk. Hypofractionated SBRT delivers ablative single doses (e.g., 18 Gy × 3) to small lung or liver tumors with cure rates rivaling surgery.

concepts.title: Targeted Therapy and the Imatinib Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
The exemplar of targeted therapy is imatinib (Gleevec), approved 2001 for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). CML is driven by the Philadelphia chromosome — t(9;22) translocation creating the BCR-ABL fusion kinase, constitutively active and necessary for the leukemic phenotype. Imatinib binds the ATP-binding pocket of ABL kinase, shutting it down. Five-year survival for chronic-phase CML went from ~30% with prior therapy to ~90% — one of the largest jumps in oncology history.

Other targeted agents reshaping practice. EGFR inhibitors (erlotinib, gefitinib, osimertinib) for EGFR-mutant NSCLC. BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib) for BRAF V600E melanoma — typically combined with MEK inhibitors (trametinib) to delay resistance. ALK inhibitors (crizotinib, alectinib, lorlatinib) for ALK-rearranged NSCLC. KRAS G12C inhibitors (sotorasib/Lumakras 2021, adagrasib 2022) — KRAS was called "undruggable" for 40 years until allele-specific covalent inhibitors broke through.

The general principle: identify a tumor-specific molecular dependency (oncogene addiction), design a drug that selectively disrupts it, and patient response correlates with biomarker status, not tissue of origin.

concepts.title: Endocrine Therapy and Antibody-Drug Conjugates
concepts.contentHtml:
Endocrine therapy exploits hormone-driven cancers. ~70% of breast cancers express estrogen receptor (ER+). Therapies: tamoxifen (a selective ER modulator, antagonist in breast tissue) — first-line adjuvant therapy since the 1980s. Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane) block peripheral estrogen synthesis in postmenopausal women. Fulvestrant degrades ER. In prostate cancer, androgen deprivation therapy (LHRH agonists like leuprolide; antiandrogens like enzalutamide; CYP17 inhibitors like abiraterone) targets the AR-driven proliferation program.

Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are a fast-growing modality. An antibody targeting a tumor antigen is covalently linked through a cleavable linker to a potent cytotoxic payload. The antibody delivers the toxin selectively; the payload kills upon internalization. Trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1, Kadcyla) — anti-HER2 antibody + microtubule poison. Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd, Enhertu) — same antibody, topoisomerase inhibitor payload, with a higher drug-to-antibody ratio and bystander effect — has become standard for HER2-low and HER2+ breast cancer. Sacituzumab govitecan targets TROP-2 in triple-negative breast cancer. ADC oncology is now where many of the new approvals are happening.

title: Immunotherapy: Checkpoints, CAR-T, and Beyond
description: Anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4, CAR-T, neoantigen vaccines, bispecifics

concepts.title: Checkpoint Inhibitors
concepts.contentHtml:
James Allison and Tasuku Honjo shared the 2018 Nobel Prize for discovering that T cells have built-in brakes — checkpoints — that tumors exploit, and that releasing those brakes unleashes anti-tumor immunity.

CTLA-4 is upregulated on activated T cells and outcompetes the costimulatory CD28 for B7 ligands on antigen-presenting cells, dampening priming. Ipilimumab (anti-CTLA-4, approved 2011 for melanoma) was the first checkpoint inhibitor to show overall survival benefit — modest median improvement, but a long tail of durable responders. The landmark melanoma trials showed ~20% of treated patients alive at 10 years, an outcome unthinkable previously.

PD-1 on T cells engages PD-L1 on tumor or stromal cells and delivers an inhibitory signal that's particularly active in the tumor microenvironment. Anti-PD-1 antibodies (pembrolizumab/Keytruda, nivolumab/Opdivo) and anti-PD-L1 antibodies (atezolizumab, durvalumab) have been approved across dozens of indications: melanoma, NSCLC, renal, urothelial, head and neck, MSI-high colorectal, Hodgkin lymphoma, hepatocellular, gastric, triple-negative breast, and counting. Combination ipilimumab + nivolumab raises response rates further at the cost of severe immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, pneumonitis, endocrinopathies) requiring steroids.

concepts.title: CAR-T and Adoptive Cell Therapy
concepts.contentHtml:
Where checkpoint inhibitors release endogenous T cells, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy engineers them. The patient's T cells are collected by leukapheresis, transduced with a lentivirus encoding a CAR — typically an anti-CD19 single-chain antibody fused to CD3ζ and CD28 or 4-1BB costimulatory domains — expanded ex vivo, and reinfused. The CAR redirects T cells to recognize CD19 on B cells (and B-cell tumors) independent of MHC.

Tisagenlecleucel (Kymriah) was approved in 2017 for relapsed/refractory pediatric B-ALL — the first CAR-T approval. Axicabtagene ciloleucel (Yescarta) followed for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Response rates in heavily pretreated, otherwise terminal patients reach 70-90%, with ~40% achieving durable complete remission. BCMA-targeted CAR-Ts (idecabtagene vicleucel, ciltacabtagene autoleucel) extended the strategy to multiple myeloma.

Toxicities are severe and characteristic. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) — massive IL-6 release; managed with the IL-6 receptor antibody tocilizumab. ICANS (immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome) — encephalopathy, sometimes fatal cerebral edema. CAR-T also fails in solid tumors so far — antigen heterogeneity, immunosuppressive TME, and trafficking limitations remain unsolved.

concepts.title: Neoantigen Vaccines, TCR-T, and Bispecifics
concepts.contentHtml:
Other immunotherapy modalities are maturing rapidly. Personalized neoantigen vaccines: sequence the tumor, predict patient-specific neoantigens that bind the patient's HLA, synthesize them as peptides or mRNAs, vaccinate. The Moderna/Merck mRNA-4157 melanoma trial (KEYNOTE-942, 2023) reported a ~44% reduction in recurrence when added to pembrolizumab — a striking signal for a Phase 2.

TCR-T cells use a transgenic T cell receptor (rather than a CAR) to target intracellular antigens presented on MHC. Afamitresgene autoleucel (afami-cel) targets MAGE-A4 in synovial sarcoma — first TCR-T approval, 2024. The challenge is HLA-restriction: each TCR works only for one HLA allele.

Bispecific T cell engagers (BiTEs / TCEs) are antibodies with two arms — one binding a tumor antigen, the other CD3 on T cells — physically tethering T cells to tumor cells. Blinatumomab (anti-CD19 × anti-CD3) was approved 2014 for B-ALL. Teclistamab (anti-BCMA × anti-CD3, 2022) for myeloma. Tarlatamab (anti-DLL3, 2024) for small-cell lung cancer — a previously hopeless disease. Bispecifics are off-the-shelf, faster than CAR-T, and increasingly central to hematologic oncology.

title: Resistance, Prevention, and Precision Oncology
description: Why drugs fail, how to prevent cancer, and the future of treatment

concepts.title: Mechanisms of Drug Resistance
concepts.contentHtml:
Effective cancer therapy almost invariably runs into resistance. Mechanisms cluster into a few archetypes. Target mutation: a single amino acid change in the drug target. The textbook case is BCR-ABL T315I — a threonine-to-isoleucine substitution at the ATP-binding pocket gatekeeper that blocks imatinib, dasatinib, and nilotinib. Ponatinib was specifically engineered to overcome T315I. EGFR T790M emerges in ~50% of patients on first-generation EGFR TKIs; osimertinib was developed against it. EGFR C797S then arises against osimertinib — the Red Queen race continues.

Alternative pathway activation: bypass the inhibited node. MET amplification rescues EGFR signaling. NRAS or BRAF mutations bypass upstream kinase blockade. Drug efflux: ABC transporters (P-glycoprotein/MDR1, BCRP) actively pump drugs out of cells; selected for under chemotherapy pressure. Lineage plasticity: prostate adenocarcinoma can transdifferentiate to AR-independent neuroendocrine cancer; lung adenocarcinoma can become small-cell. The drug-targetable phenotype is replaced by a different cell state entirely.

Resistance is rarely single-mechanism in a real patient. ctDNA studies often reveal multiple coexisting resistance mutations across subclones, hence the appeal of combination therapy.

concepts.title: Prevention and Screening
concepts.contentHtml:
The most effective cancer interventions are preventive. Tobacco control — smoking causes ~85% of lung cancers; cessation cuts risk by ~90% over 15 years. HPV vaccination (Gardasil) prevents cervical cancer (and head/neck cancers) caused by HPV-16/18. Cervical cancer rates in vaccinated cohorts have fallen dramatically; Australia is on track to eliminate the disease by 2035. Hepatitis B vaccination prevents most hepatocellular carcinoma in endemic regions.

Screening aims to catch disease early enough to cure. Mammography for breast cancer, colonoscopy for colorectal cancer, low-dose CT for lung cancer in heavy smokers (NLST, 20% mortality reduction), and Pap smears for cervical cancer all save lives. But screening has costs.

Overdiagnosis — detection of cancers that would never have caused symptoms in the patient's lifetime — is real and substantial. Estimates for prostate cancer (PSA screening) and thyroid cancer suggest 30-50% of screen-detected tumors fall into this category. Each overdiagnosed cancer leads to surgery, radiation, or anxiety with no benefit. The mammography ROC curve trades sensitivity (cancers caught) against specificity (false positives leading to biopsy). Reasonable people disagree on optimal screening intervals — the evidence base is genuinely contested.

concepts.title: Precision Oncology and Trial Design
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern oncology is reorganizing itself around mutation rather than tissue. Basket trials enroll patients across cancer types based on a shared molecular alteration. The classic example: larotrectinib for NTRK-fusion-positive tumors, approved 2018 across all solid tumors regardless of origin — pediatric infantile fibrosarcoma, salivary gland MASC, GI stromal tumors all share NTRK fusions and all respond. Umbrella trials reverse the design — a single tumor type stratified into multiple treatment arms by molecular profile (e.g., NCI-MATCH, BATTLE for lung cancer).

Tissue-agnostic FDA approvals now exist for: pembrolizumab (MSI-high or TMB-high), larotrectinib and entrectinib (NTRK fusions), selpercatinib (RET fusions), dabrafenib + trametinib (BRAF V600E), dostarlimab (dMMR endometrial → broader). The trend will continue as more rare driver alterations are characterized.

Pediatric and rare cancers benefit asymmetrically from this paradigm — they were previously orphaned by tissue-based development, but a fusion-defined sarcoma in a child can now access the same drug as a fusion-defined lung cancer in an adult. Adaptive platform trials (I-SPY 2 for breast cancer; Lung-MAP) drop ineffective arms and add new ones in real time, accelerating learning. The ultimate vision — match every patient to the right therapy from a sequenced tumor — remains aspirational but is closer than it has ever been.
